logos.r4-01: The source's own heavy two-tone S, with the bowls pulled far enough apart that the break at the waist finally reads. In the source that gap is swallowed by the stroke weight.
logos.r4-02: The two halves kept close but built at different sizes, so the break announces itself by mismatch rather than by distance — two things not yet the same.
logos.r4-03: Weight taken right down so the S reads as a letter first and the gap becomes a crisp deliberate slot. Tests whether the idea survives without the heavy stroke doing the work.
logos.r4-04: The break relocated to the outer terminals — the halves meet cleanly at the waist and stay open at the ends, so the mark is joined in the middle and unfinished at its edges.
logos.r4-05: One straight diagonal cut sliced across an otherwise whole letter — the gap stops being a space between two parts and becomes a slot through a single object.
logos.r4-06: Out of register — the halves are not merely apart but shifted sideways, so the mark reads as sync attempted and missed rather than sync waiting to happen.
logos.r4-07: Departure — the letter is dropped and only the unfinished circle is kept: two facing half-rings with the gap between them, a ring that has not closed yet.
logos.r4-08: Departure — the gap promoted to the entire subject: two solid slabs and the bright slot between them, with nothing else left in the frame. The lowest element count in the batch.
logos.r4-09: Departure — the gap read as the moment of contact rather than as absence: the same two halves with one small node bridging the space where the link is made.
logos.r4-10: Departure — a sequence rather than a pair: three bars with two gaps sliding into one line, so sync reads as several things arriving together instead of two halves meeting.
